title: Many agents on purpose
bridge: A workflow script is like a file that orchestrates a few Promise.all() calls. Except: each promise is a whole subagent, and the script holds the plan instead of the model. Date.now() and Math.random() throw inside it, so a run can be replayed from its saved results.
intro: Research is where extra agents help most: four cheap readers in parallel give the planner a wide view for little cost. Writing code is where they hurt: one writer per change. This lesson shows the Workflow tool and the script API (agent, parallel, pipeline, phase). It shows how to run a saved workflow from a session, and how to size a run on purpose.

picture.caption: Nova calls the Workflow tool with a saved script. The runtime fans out helpers, then planners, then a judge, and returns one result.

steps.text: calls Workflow with name 'nova-research' and args
loads the saved script and runs it in the background

sections.h: When many agents help, and when they do not
p: A workflow is a JavaScript script that starts many subagents and holds the plan itself: loops, fan-out, what to merge. Only the final return enters the calling session's context. That is the win: four readers can each read 100K tokens and the planner sees one list of pointers.

It helps for research: where is the code, which tests, similar PRs, the brain. It helps for independent plans with a judge on fuzzy tickets, and for review panels on big diffs. It does not help for writing code: parallel writers conflict. One writer per change stays the rule.
Nova decides when to use one, guided by one line in the plan-and-grill skill. The harness never forces it.

callout.text: One writer per change. A workflow may read, plan, judge and review in parallel; it never edits the same repo from several agents.

p: A script starts with export const meta: name, description, and the phase titles, as a plain object literal. Then a body in plain JavaScript with top-level await. agent(prompt, opts) starts one subagent and returns its text, or an object if opts.schema is given.
parallel(thunks) runs functions at once and waits for all. phase(title) groups the agents that follow in the progress view. log(text) shows a line. args is whatever the caller passed.

An agent() that is stopped or dies on an API error returns null, so results are filtered with .filter(Boolean). Scripts are not TypeScript: no type annotations. No imports, no file system: agents do the work.
sections.because: We write the lab script first because the API is small, and seeing one whole script makes the real ones readable.

notes.text: A pure literal: no variables, no spreads. The name is how a session calls it.
A JSON Schema, by hand. Scripts cannot import zod; keep schemas small.
parallel takes functions (thunks), not promises. Each thunk starts one agent.
schema makes agent() return an object. model and effort per call; phase pins it to a group.
Plain JavaScript between agents: filter nulls, add up. No Date.now(), no Math.random().
The return value is the tool result Nova sees.

sections.h: Run a saved workflow from a session
p: Saved workflows live in .claude/workflows/ of the project or ~/.claude/workflows/ of the user. In the sandbox image Packer bakes Nova's scripts into ~/.claude/workflows/ of the VM user, not into fcp. settingSources must include the matching source for them to load.

Under dontAsk the Workflow tool itself must be in allowedTools, or the launch is refused like any other call. The settings option can turn workflows on and set the size guideline. A PostToolUse hook on Workflow prints the tool result, which carries the runId.

The settings option takes a Settings object or a string. A string is read as the path to a settings JSON file, like the --settings flag of the claude CLI. Some ticket sketches (G4-01, walkthrough g4-5) write JSON.stringify({...}) there. We pass the object, because TypeScript checks its keys.
sections.because: We allow the Workflow tool explicitly because in a headless session nobody can approve the launch prompt a person would see.

notes.text: Narrowing on hook_event_name instead of a cast: TypeScript then knows tool_response exists.
'project' loads .claude/workflows/ next to cwd. The spike uses ['user', 'project'] for ~/.claude/workflows/.
The lab's agents only read, so Read, Glob and Grep are enough for them too.
settings is the flag layer: highest priority among user-controlled settings. Here it is an object; a string would be a file path. Workflows are on for paid plans; Pro turns them on in /config.
The runtime caps concurrent agents at this number; the VM's CPUs decide the value: 3 lite, 6 full, 12 wide.
modelUsage lists haiku next to opus: workflow agents are counted in the session's cost.

p: Three things bound a run. CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS caps how many agents run at the same moment.

The harness sets 3, 6 or 12 by VM size, because agents are processes and the VM has that many CPUs. workflowSizeGuideline (small: fewer than 5 agents) is advice to the model that writes a script, not a cap. The runtime also caps a run at 1,000 agents and a parallel() or pipeline() call at 4,096 items.

A workflow agent inherits the session's tools and permissions. It cannot start a new run: there is no orchestrator access in the VM, and workflow() nests one level only. Workflow agents' calls go to the gateway with the same run token, so they count toward the ticket's cost and the backstop.

callout.text: Run a workflow on a small slice first (one folder, one question). The /workflows view in interactive Claude Code shows each agent's tokens as it runs.

p: Four questions, four Haiku helpers in parallel, each returning file:line pointers in a fixed schema. The prompts stay under 100K tokens each. The brain question says 'skipped' until the kb skill exists (G6). 'Similar past PRs' uses gh through the broker, read-only.
If the ticket is not fuzzy the script returns the notes and stops. Nova decides fuzzy from the readiness verdict (size: fuzzy).
sections.because: We fan out research because reading is where extra agents add width for little cost. The planner needs width before it needs depth.

notes.text: Three phase titles, matched exactly by the phase() calls below.
Every helper returns { pointers: [{ where, why }] }: a shape the planner can read without parsing prose.
The helper reports 'skipped' when it cannot search the brain. No silent gaps.
args.ticket is the ticket text Nova passed in. haiku at medium: the helper row of the routing table.
A bigger ticket that is not fuzzy stops here: notes only.

sections.h: nova-research.js, part 2: three plans and a judge
p: For fuzzy tickets three planners write a plan each from a different angle: the smallest safe change, risk first, the user first. Each returns a Plan in the G4-07 schema, passed in as args.planSchema, so the shape is the same one the harness validates. A judge picks one and grafts the best ideas from the others.
The judge inherits the main loop's model, Opus 5.5, at medium. The planners inherit it too; only effort and schema are set.
sections.because: We make independent plans and judge them. For fuzzy work, three angles with a judge beat one plan polished on its own.

code.text:
phase('Plans')
const ANGLES = ['the smallest safe change', 'risk first: what could break', 'the user first: every screen state']
const plans = await parallel(ANGLES.map((angle) => () =>
  agent(`Write a plan for this ticket, thinking ${angle}.\nTicket:\n${args.ticket}\nNotes:\n${JSON.stringify(notes)}`,
    { schema: args.planSchema, phase: 'Plans' })))

phase('Judge')
const plan = await agent(
  `Pick the plan a reviewer and a tester would trust most; graft good ideas from the others. Return the final plan.\n${JSON.stringify(plans.filter(Boolean))}`,
  { schema: args.planSchema, effort: 'medium', phase: 'Judge' })
return { notes, plan }

notes.text: Three angles, three independent contexts. They never see each other's plan.
args.planSchema is z.toJSONSchema(Plan) computed by the harness: one schema everywhere.
The judge sees all surviving plans at once; this is the one place a barrier (parallel) is right.
Nova receives notes and one plan; the harness runs Plan.safeParse on it.

p: On big diffs one reviewer misses things. The panel runs five lenses: correctness, security, conventions, plan coverage and tests. Then a skeptic per important finding tries to refute it. A skeptic must show the problem at file:line, or the finding is dropped.

pipeline(items, stage1, stage2) runs each item through the stages with no barrier between them. The security lens can be in the skeptic stage while conventions is still reviewing. The panel runs from the read-only reviewer session (Read, Grep, Glob, Workflow), so lenses and skeptics cannot edit anything.
When to use it: diffs over about 300 changed lines, 8 or more files, or a risky area. One reviewer otherwise.
sections.because: We add a skeptic per finding because a panel that only finds cries wolf. A panel that also refutes finds more and cries wolf less.

code.text:
const LENSES = [
  { name: 'correctness', opts: {} },
  { name: 'security', opts: {} },
  { name: 'conventions (frontend/AGENTS.md and the Byte playbook)', opts: { model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low' } },
  { name: 'plan coverage: is every plan item and QA check done?', opts: {} },
  { name: 'tests: do they read what the user sees, and could they fail?', opts: {} },
]

const reviewed = await pipeline(LENSES,
  (lens) => agent(`Review the diff in /run/nova/review/diff.patch through the ${lens.name} lens.\nTicket:\n${args.ticket}`,
    { schema: FINDINGS, phase: 'Lenses', ...lens.opts }),
  (found) => parallel((found?.findings ?? []).filter((f) => f.severity === 'important').map((f) => () =>
    agent(`Try to refute this finding. Read the code at ${f.path}:${f.line}. If you cannot show the problem, refuted=true.\n${f.body}`,
      { schema: VERDICT, phase: 'Skeptics' }).then((v) => (v && !v.refuted ? { ...f, evidence: v.evidence } : null)))))

const kept = reviewed.flat().filter(Boolean)
log(`${kept.length} important findings survived the skeptics`)
return { findings: kept }

notes.text: The conventions lens is cheap work: Sonnet at low. The others inherit Opus 5.5.
pipeline: stage 1 per lens, stage 2 per lens's findings. No waiting for the slowest lens.
Stage 2 fans out again: one skeptic per important finding, in parallel.
A refuted finding becomes null and is dropped; a surviving one carries the skeptic's evidence.
log() tells the person what was dropped: no silent caps.

callout.text: FINDINGS and VERDICT (defined above the body in the file) are hand-written JSON Schemas, like POINTERS. Scripts cannot import zod.

p: The Workflow tool result carries a runId. If the session is killed mid-workflow, resume the session (p8-6) and call Workflow again with the same script and resumeFromRunId.
Completed agent() calls with an unchanged prompt return their saved result at once. Only the first changed call and everything after it run live. Same session only.

That is why Date.now() and Math.random() throw in a script: a replay must build the same prompts. The spike checks exactly this, and writes a go or no-go for G4-09 and G4-19 in ai-agents/docs/spikes/workflows-in-the-vm.md.

callout.text: If a headless session exits before the workflow ends, the spike says to try CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS=0 and note it.

quiz.q: What is the difference between parallel() and pipeline()?

options.text: parallel waits for all thunks (a barrier); pipeline runs each item through all stages with no barrier
options.why: Use pipeline by default; use parallel only when a later step needs all results together, like a judge.

options.text: pipeline runs agents one at a time; parallel runs them at once
options.why: Both run agents concurrently; the difference is whether stages wait for each other.

options.text: parallel is for Haiku, pipeline for Opus
options.why: Models are set per agent() call; neither function cares.

quiz.q: Why do Date.now() and Math.random() throw inside a workflow script?

options.text: Scripts have no access to Node APIs at all
options.why: JSON, Math and Array work; these two are blocked on purpose.

options.text: So a resumed run builds the same prompts and can reuse completed agents' saved results
options.why: resumeFromRunId caches by (prompt, opts); a changing prompt would rerun everything.

options.text: Because agents run on other machines with other clocks
options.why: Agents run in the same VM; the reason is replay, not clocks.

quiz.q: The plan says a change touches 12 files. Should Nova write the code with a workflow?

options.text: Yes, one agent per file is faster
options.why: Parallel writers conflict and nobody holds the whole change; one writer per change is a wall.

options.text: No; use a workflow for the research before and the review panel after, and one writer for the change
options.why: Workflows add width where reading helps; the edit stays with one context.
The cap bounds resources; it does not make parallel editing safe.

words.plain: The built-in tool that runs a workflow script in the background and returns its result and a runId.
A plain JavaScript file with export const meta and a body that calls agent(), parallel(), pipeline(), phase().
Starts one subagent with a prompt; returns its text, or an object when a schema is given; null if it died.
Runs a list of functions at once and waits for all of them: a barrier.
Runs each item through stages independently; an item can be in stage 2 while another is in stage 1.
Names the group the following agents appear under in the progress view.
The id of one workflow run; pass it as resumeFromRunId to replay with cached results.

tickets.why: The spike runs a workflow headless in a lite VM behind the gateway; this lesson's lab is the laptop version of it.
nova-research.js is explained line by line here: helpers in parallel, three plans, a judge.
nova-review-panel.js is the pipeline example: lenses, then a skeptic per finding.

remember: Fan out to read, plan and review; never to write. The script holds the plan, agent() returns data, and only the return value enters Nova's context.
